Shogi is Japanese chess on a 9x9 board. Sente (the first player) sits at the bottom and moves first. Each piece moves in its own way; switch the piece style to Symbols to see arrows for every piece.

Captured pieces are kept in your hand. On your turn you may instead drop a piece from your hand onto any empty square, and it becomes yours. Drops have limits: no two unpromoted pawns of yours in one column (nifu), no piece dropped where it could never move, and no pawn drop that gives checkmate.

When a piece moves into, within, or out of the last three rows it may promote; pawns, lances and knights must promote when they could not move any more. Promoted silver, knight, lance and pawn move like a gold general; a bishop becomes a horse and a rook a dragon.

Trap the enemy king (checkmate) to win. Repeating the same position four times is a draw, unless one side was giving perpetual check, which loses. If both kings reach the enemy camp, you can declare a win on your turn with enough pieces (28 points for Sente, 27 for Gote; rooks and bishops count 5, others 1).

Mini Shogi is shogi on a 5x5 board with a rook, bishop, gold, silver, king and pawn each. Sente (the first player) sits at the bottom and moves first.

Captured pieces are kept in your hand. On your turn you may instead drop a piece from your hand onto any empty square, and it becomes yours. You may not drop a pawn in a column where you already have one (nifu), drop a pawn where it could not move, or drop a pawn that gives checkmate.

Reaching the far row lets a piece promote (a pawn must). Promoted pawn and silver move like a gold; a bishop becomes a horse and a rook a dragon.

Trap the enemy king (checkmate) to win. Four repetitions of a position is a draw, unless one side kept giving check, which loses.

Did you know? Shogi is the only major chess game where captured pieces return to play, which is why there are no draws by lack of material.
